definition: Inviolable means never to be broken or dishonored.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word inviolable. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know inviolable should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: In the lifeboat drills one rule was inviolable: crew boards last.
A respected rule is honored by most people most of the time, and that is all it asks; inviolable stands far above it — a rule no one would even think to test.
A binding rule must be obeyed while it stands, yet binding deals are renegotiated every season; inviolable is the far rung — breaking it is not renegotiation, it is desecration.

Sacred means held holy — set apart for reverence, so that mistreating it feels like sacrilege. Inviolable borrows that holiness and lends it to rules, promises, and rights: the thing itself may be plain paper, but breaking it is desecration. Sacred names the reverence; inviolable names the ban on breaking.

Unbreakable is the plain physical twin — the word for locks, vaults, and codes that force cannot crack. Inviolable does its work in the moral world of treaties, confidences, and oaths, where breaking is perfectly possible but utterly unthinkable. Call the padlock unbreakable; call the promise inviolable.

Parking across the fire lane is a violation — a small rule broken, with violare sitting inside the word.
Inviolable means never to be broken or dishonored.
On the glacier, the rope team's law is inviolable: no one unclips, ever — not for a photograph, not for a dropped mitten, not for the last easy hundred meters.
Guides who shrug at most regulations go quiet about this one; in eighty years of the hut's logbook, not one entry marks an exception.
Inviolable stacks a claim on top of strict.
Breaking a strict rule costs you something; breaking an inviolable one is unthinkable — the rule carries a kind of holiness.
Violare, 'to break, to profane,' hides in the middle: what is inviolable must never be profaned, whether it is a treaty, a confidence, or the rope.
Inviolable wraps a rule, promise, or right in something like holiness: breaking it is desecration, not infraction.
Its unit-mate impregnable protects places from capture; inviolable protects covenants from betrayal.
If exceptions get granted on busy days, the word is overclaiming.

When Marisol joined the paper, the senior editor walked her through one rule before showing her where the coffee was: a source's name is never given up.
The style guide devoted three pages to commas and a single sentence to sources, but nobody doubted which sentence mattered.
That autumn a subpoena arrived, and Marisol watched the newsroom treat the rule as inviolable rather than merely inconvenient.
The editor spent nine days in custody rather than answer the court's question, and came back to a standing ovation.
Deadlines slipped and expense forms wandered, the editor liked to say, but in forty years no one at the paper had tested this one rule.
